reading.body:
Vermont has introduced 64 AI-related bills since January 2025, and the largest cluster regulates what AI says and decides rather than how much compute it consumes.

The bills group into recognizable families. Chatbots and companion chatbots draw at least four separate measures. Mental health applications draw three. Elections and synthetic media draw three more. Liability for developers and deployers, automated decision systems, employment screening, rental pricing, health coverage decisions, and consumer data privacy each draw their own. Two bills address physical infrastructure directly: S0205 proposes a temporary moratorium on AI data centers, and H0727 addresses sustainable data center deployment. H0720 proposes a Cloud Computing Public Utility Act. That is the full extent of the compute and power thread in this data.

For AI specifically, the pattern is that a small, rural state with no significant data center footprint is legislating the application layer heavily and the infrastructure layer lightly. The moratorium and public utility bills exist, but they sit among sixty-plus proposals aimed at disclosure, liability, and privacy. If the binding constraint on AI scaling is power and buildings, this legislative record does not yet treat it that way.

What the data does not show is enactment. These are bill introductions with dates, not laws, and no vote counts, committee outcomes, or vetoes appear. It also does not show whether the data center measures advanced or stalled. One news item, dated September 2026, reports governors unsettled by AI advancements, with no further detail. The count of 64 is a count of introduced bills, not of passed policy.

The 64 bills are not spread evenly across the two years. Forty-one carry 2026 dates and twenty-three carry 2025 dates, so the volume of AI-related introductions roughly doubled between the first year and the second. The 2026 cluster is also denser in January, with sixteen bills dated between January 5 and January 28, which is the signature of a session opening rather than a gradual accumulation of concern.

The subject matter splits along a different line than the calendar. Bills about what AI outputs, meaning chatbots, synthetic media, digital replicas, and generated images, tend to be short and narrow, often covering a single product category. Bills about what AI is, meaning liability standards, developer and deployer duties, and automated decision systems, are broader and appear in both years. The infrastructure thread is the thinnest of all: three bills out of 64, and two of them, S0205 and H0727, are the only ones that name data centers at all.

Vermont's bill count is high relative to its size, but the data cannot say whether that reflects legislative capacity or simply that a small state with a part-time legislature can introduce many bills cheaply. What the data does show is that the state is writing rules for AI applications it can observe, such as chatbots and pricing algorithms, while leaving the physical layer mostly untouched. The one moratorium bill, S0205, is dated January 5, 2026, the earliest date in the 2026 cluster, which places it at the front of the session rather than at the end.

How many Vermont AI bills became law?
The data does not hold this. It lists bill introductions with dates and titles, and contains no vote counts, committee outcomes, signatures, or vetoes.

Which Vermont AI bills are about data centers or power?
Three. S0205 proposes a temporary moratorium on AI data centers and a report on their construction and operation, H0727 addresses sustainable data center deployment, and H0720 proposes a Cloud Computing Public Utility Act.

What is the most common subject among these bills?
Chatbots and companion chatbots, with at least four separate measures: H0804, H0784, H0783, and H0829, which covers robocalls using an artificial voice. Mental health applications and elections each draw three.

When were most of these bills introduced?
In 2026. Forty-one of the 64 carry 2026 dates, and sixteen of those fall in January 2026 alone. The remaining twenty-three are dated 2025.

Does the data show any federal or multi-state action on AI?
No. Every entry is a Vermont bill with a Legiscan link, plus one news item dated September 14, 2026, headlined "AI advancements leave governors on edge," which carries no further detail.

Are there bills on AI in health care and employment?
Yes. H0776 covers AI in health care coverage decisions, H0814 covers neurological rights and AI in health and human services, and H0816 and S0241 and H0644 regulate AI in mental health services. H0714 covers automated employment decision making for State employees, and H0262 restricts electronic monitoring of employees and employment-related automated decision systems.
